{"result":"# The Rust Programming Language and Memory Safety

Rust balances performance, type safety, concurrency, and memory safety [1]. Its design raises a question every systems programmer eventually faces: how do you write fast, low-level code without introducing memory bugs?

Memory safety protects programs from bugs such as buffer overflows and dangling pointers [3]. Languages like C, C++, and Fortran allow arbitrary pointer arithmetic without bounds checking, which makes them memory-unsafe [3]. Java takes a different route, checking array bounds and pointer dereferences at runtime [3].

Rust was initially developed by Graydon Hoare starting in 2006, and Mozilla Research sponsored it from 2009 [2]. Version 1.0 arrived in 2015 [2]. Syntactically, Rust resembles C++, yet it guarantees memory safety without a garbage collector [2].

Rust also draws on functional programming, adopting immutability, higher-order functions, algebraic data types, and pattern matching [1]. Rather than classes or inheritance, it relies on structs, enums, traits, and methods [1]. Together, these choices show how a language can keep memory safe while staying close to the metal.","trace":[{"name":"Draft","status":"ok","ms":4413,"detail":"171 words: The Rust Programming Language and Memory Safety Rust balances performance, type safety,…","tokens":2662,"cost":0.00065241}],"usage":{"prompt_tokens":1680,"completion_tokens":982,"total_tokens":2662,"cost":0.00065241},"model":"anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5","newestModel":"anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5","modelCheck":"match","totalMs":4413}

{"text":"Rust balances performance, type safety, concurrency, and memory safety [1]. How can a programmer write fast, low-level code without introducing memory bugs? Memory safety guards programs against bugs such as buffer overflows and dangling pointers [3]. Languages such as C, C++, and Fortran allow arbitrary pointer arithmetic without bounds checking, which makes them memory-unsafe [3]. Java takes a different route, checking array bounds and pointer dereferences at runtime [3].

Graydon Hoare began developing Rust in 2006, and Mozilla Research sponsored the project from 2009 [2]. Version 1.0 arrived in 2015 [2]. Syntactically, Rust resembles C++, yet it avoids a garbage collector [2].

Rust also draws on functional programming, adopting immutability, algebraic data types, and pattern matching [1]. Rather than classes and inheritance, it relies on structs, enums, and traits [1]. Together, these choices show how a language can stay memory safe while remaining close to the metal.","sources":"[1] Wikipedia: Rust (programming language)
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rust_%28programming_language%29
Summary: Rust is a general-purpose programming language that emphasizes performance, type safety, concurrency, and memory safety. Rust supports multiple programming paradigms. It was influenced by ideas from functional programming, including immutability, higher-order functions, algebraic data types, and pattern matching. Rust also provides structs, enums, traits, and methods as alternatives to traditional object-oriented programming, without relying on classes or inheritance.

[2] Wikipedia: Outline of the Rust programming language
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outline_of_the_Rust_programming_language
Summary: The following outline is provided as an overview of and topical guide to Rust: Rust is a multi-paradigm programming language emphasizing performance, memory safety, and concurrency. Rust was initially developed by Graydon Hoare starting in 2006, later sponsored and maintained by Mozilla Research starting in 2009, and first publicly released in 2010, with version 1.0 released in 2015. Rust is syntactically similar to C++ but guarantees memory safety without needing a garbage collector.

[3] Wikipedia: Memory safety
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memory_safety
Summary: Memory safety is the state of being protected from various software bugs and security vulnerabilities when dealing with memory access, such as buffer overflows and dangling pointers. For example, Java is memory-safe because its runtime error detection checks array bounds and pointer dereferences. By contrast, programming languages like C, C++, and Fortran allow arbitrary pointer arithmetic with pointers implemented as direct memory addresses with no provision for bounds checking, making them memory-unsafe.
